results.title: Estimating Task Durations
results.content: # Estimating Task Durations. Estimating task durations is one of the fundamental parts of project management. It involves the estimation of the amount of time required by a certain project activity given the available resources. In the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK), the main output of the ***Estimate Activity Duration*** process are *Activity Duration Estimates*. ## Activity Duration Estimates. The main output of the *Estimate Activity Durations* process is a duration for each task. This is called ***Bottom Up Estimating***, whereby each task is given an estimate and the total is rolled up into the overall project estimate. The duration estimates can also be a range, for example 4-6 days, or a probability, for example 4 days @ 90%. But I would not recommend this type of scheduling unless you are a professional and understand the use of earned value analysis and project control with variable activity durations. I generally support this view, but this is often not practical and project team members do not want to be bogged down with endless duration estimates. ## How to Estimate Durations. To estimate an activity duration, proceed through this list and perform each one, skipping the ones that do not apply to your project:. A second common method for estimating task durations requires that the work be drilled down into a unit cost, such as a time per square foot of concrete pouring. For example, maybe this carpet installer frequently underestimates duration, or the past experience estimates are skewed by a certain piece of data. For example, let’s say the expected duration of the task *Place Rebar* is 6 days (m = 6), and you figure there is significant potential for delays. The beta distribution yields 7 days as the task duration you should use. If you add up all of the durations (∑m) and standard deviations (∑σ) for each task, you will have the total project duration as well as it’s standard deviation. If the chance of delaying the concrete pouring by a day (plus all the other risks) is great enough, a task duration of 2 days or more days should be used. results.title: Wall-clock time vs. user time
results.content: 1. **Wall-clock time**: this is the amount of time it takes between now and finishing a task, according to the clock on the wall. 2. **User time**: this is the amount of time you spend actively engaging with / working on a task. Maybe this typically takes me 5 hours of work sat at my desk, researching and then writing (_user time)_, and I expect to finish it by this Sunday evening (my measure of _wall-clock time_). This will mean any _user time_ you spend on each project will have a high marginal benefit, minimising total user time spent, even if it means that projects will take longer from start to finish.). **Taking 30 minutes to plan the day’s tasks** (this is likely to make you more efficient, thus reducing the total _user time_ you need to spend on your tasks, but you will miss your morning deadlines because of the 30 minute set-back early on). * **Banging your head on the wall**(trying to complete a task that you’re finding very difficult may take a lot of your user time, but because everyone else is busy in meetings you can’t complete it in time for the deadline if you wait for them)****_vs_. You’ll notice from the list that the things that reduce wall-clock time at the expense of increasing user time are (mostly) features of disorganised, unproductive schedules. If you are (repeatedly) having to increase the amount of user time you spend on a problem in order to reduce the wall-clock time, this can drastically reduce your overall productivity. But even if you don’t feel like taking a stance on whether it’s “better” to avoid increasing user time in order to meet wall-clock deadlines, it definitely seems useful to be _aware_ of what you’re doing when you make those trade-offs. That is, there are things you can do that will reduce _both_ the user time and wall-clock time for a given task: deep work, getting enough sleep, reducing distractions, avoiding rapid task-switching, … Even having tight deadlines can help on both fronts, thanks to “Parkinson’s Law” — the psychological pressure of a time constraint can force you to be more productive, thus reducing user time as well as wall-clock time.

results.title: Thinking About Elapsed Durations | MPUG | MPUG
results.content: When you enter a regular *Duration* value on a task with no resources assigned, Microsoft Project schedules the task according to the schedule shown on the *Project Calendar*. When you enter an *Elapsed Duration* value on a task, however, Microsoft Project schedules the task as 24/hours per day and 7 days/week, and ignores all nonworking time, such as weekends and company holidays. You could use an *Elapsed Duration* value for a task that needs to run continuously without a break, 24 hours/day and 365 days/year. So, if I enter a *Duration* value of *10 days*, Microsoft Project schedules the task for 10 consecutive ***working days***, and does not schedule the task on weekends on company holidays. If I enter a *Duration* value of *10 eDays*, the schedules the task for 10 consecutive ***24-hour calendar days***, ignoring nonworking time on weekends and company holidays. Notice that the Design 2 task finishes two days earlier than the Design 1 task because of the *Elapsed Duration* value I entered for the Design 2 task. Because an Elapsed Duration runs 24 hours/day and 365 days/week, and ignores nonworking time such as weekends and company holidays, you should not assign human resources to a task with an Elapsed Duration. This is because Microsoft Project will assign the human resource to work 24/hours per day on any task with an Elapsed Duration. * When you create a regular *Duration* value in *Weeks*, Microsoft Project assumes that a week consists of **5 working days**. * When you enter a *Duration* value in *eWeeks*, Microsoft Project assumes that a week consists of **7 calendar days**. * When you enter a *Duration* value in *Months*, Microsoft Project assumes that a month consists of ***20 working days***. * When you enter a *Duration* value in *eMonths*, Microsoft Project assumes that a month consists of ***30 calendar days***. However, keep in mind this value only impacts tasks in which you enter a regular *Duration* in *Months*, and not an *Elapsed Duration* entered in *eMonths*. * Do not assign human resources to tasks with an *Elapsed Duration* because Microsoft Project will assign the resource to work 24 hours/day and 365/days per year.

Notifications You must be signed in to change notification settings. # oleiade/durations. ## Folders and files. ## Repository files navigation. # durations. A python durations parsing library, providing a straight forward api to parse durations string representations such as '1d' or '1 day 2 hours' or '2 days 3h 26m 52s' and convert them to numeric value. It's easier, and more straight forward to read a duration in it's human form (at least for a human), as an expression rather than an amount. When writing configuration files for example:. is easier to understand for a human than. To parse a duration string representation, just instantiate a Duration object, and let it work for you. A Duration representation is composed of as many pairs as you need to express it:. * A value is an integer amount. * A scale is a duration unit in it's short or long form (both singular and plural). * Duration pairs can be separated with sep characters and expressions such as "," or "and". 1d 2 days 2 days and 4 hours 4M, 22d and 6hours ... #### Scales reference. Century scale formats: 'c', 'century', 'centuries' Decade scale formats: 'D', 'decade', 'decades' Year scale formats: 'y', 'year', 'Year' Month scale formats: 'M', 'month', 'months' Week scale formats: 'w', 'week', 'weeks' Day scale formats: 'd', 'day', 'days' Hour scale formats: 'h', 'hour', 'hours' Minute scale formats:'m', 'minute', 'minutes' Second scale formats: 's', 'second', 'seconds' Milisecond scale formats: 'ms', 'milisecond', 'miliseconds'. #### A good example worths it all. >>> from durations import Duration>>> one_hour = '1hour'>>> one_hour_duration = Duration one_hour>>> one_hour_duration to_seconds3600.0>>> one_hour_duration to_minutes60.0 # You can even compose durations in their short # and long variations>>> two_days_three_hours ='2 days, 3h'>>> two_days_three_hours_duration = Duration two_days_three_hours>>> two_days_three_hours_duration to_seconds183600.0>>> two_days_three_hours_duration to_hours51.0.
